newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's tribals relish full voting rights.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's tribals relish full voting rights.

text.p: The crackle of rifle fire and the crash of rockets usually means that tribesmen in Pakistan's frontier areas near Afghanistan are settling scores.
This time the shooting was to celebrate the granting of universal adult suffrage for the first time to the 3.4 million residents of the Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA).
Men and women aged 21 or over will go to the polls on Monday just like their compatriots in the rest of Pakistan.
"This is indeed a big step," said Latif Afridi, ex-president of the Peshawar High Court Bar and candidate in Khyber Agency.

"After 50 years the Pakistan government has acknowledged that the tribal people are neither morons nor insane and are entitled to vote like any other citizen," he said, striding through crowds of tribespeople in the Chura Valley, where troops demolished heroin processing facilities in December.
FATA's special status dates back to the days of the British Empire, when Sir Mortimer Durand drew a line between British India and Afghanistan in 1880-84, known as the Durand Line.
It served as a front line against an expansionist Tsarist Russia in the late 19th century and in the 1980s against Soviet troops occupying Afghanistan.
When Pakistan was created in 1947, it inherited British treaties that gave tribes autonomy in return for their loyalty.

Successive governments resisted demands for universal suffrage, sometimes jailing its advocates. FATA's eight National Assembly members were previously chosen by about 37,000 hand-picked maliks, or tribal elders, who were on government stipends from the Political Agents ruling the area.
But in December President Farooq Leghari and his caretaker government issued an ordinance granting universal suffrage and registered 1.6 million tribal voters in less than two weeks.
"We are surprised at the big turn-out for registration," said a senior Home and Tribal Affairs Department official.
Even more surprising, 400,000 tribal women managed to register as voters in defiance of age-old traditions in a deeply conservative and strongly Islamic society.

Some Moslem clerics and tribal elders have inveighed against the idea of women voting as "exposure to strangers" and a big, all-male tribal gathering in Khyber Agency last month unanimously voted to bar women from casting their ballots.

"Voting is a fundamental right," agreed Maulana Abdul Hadi, who heads Tanzim Ittehad-i-Ulema Qabail, a council of clerics that the government disbanded last year on charges that it was running a parallel administration to enforce Islamic Sharia law.
"But our Pashtun values do not allow us to let our women go to polling stations. We are just not used to it. It is un-Islamic. Women need not cast their votes," Hadi said.

However, for tribesmen and the authorities alike, the main bone of contention is not women's rights, but the narcotics trade that thrives in these wild and lawless mountains close to Afghanistan, source of much of the world's illicit opium.

"In modern times, the tribals are not willing to allow construction of a road to the inaccessible Tirah Valley which they feel would eventually bring the government presence and ultimately end their independence," Afridi said.
Several government attempts to gain access to the valley were fiercely resisted, but in December the authorities sent a military expedition to destroy heroin laboratories there.
"We are all against drugs, but we must be given alternative means to earn bread and butter for our children," Afridi said at a public meeting in Chura Valley, scene of the raid.

Drug money has played a major role in tribal affairs and politics in the past. Haji Ayub Afridi, a drug baron now convicted and imprisoned in the United States, bought his way into the Pakistani parliament in the 1988 elections.
His grandson Noor Alam, an engineer and candidate in Monday's polls, has rounded off his election rallies with collective prayers for the release of his grandfather.
In granting full voting rights, the government hopes to bring tribespeople into the national fold, start a dialogue with their elected representatives and open up tribal no-go areas.

"Adult franchise is the first step towards initiating much-needed socio-economic reforms in the tribal areas," Afridi said. "We were never able to highlight our problems. Hopefully there will now be a meaningful dialogue."
